meta.title: Who really said "St Paul's Cathedral Is Amusing, Awful, and Artificial"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Charles II's 1675 warrant called Wren's design "very artificial, proper, and useful." The three-adjective version first appears in 1938 - credited to King James.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'St Paul's Cathedral Is Amusing, Awful, and Artificial'?
meta.ogDescription: The royal warrant said "very artificial, proper, and useful." The famous three-adjective wording is a 20th-century retelling.

answer.label: Not Charles II’s words — a 20th-century retelling
answer.authorDates: 1630–1685 · King of England, Scotland and Ireland
answer.sourceLine: The king really did praise Wren’s design, and he really did use the word artificial — but in a warrant, not a quip. The document signed at Whitehall on 14 May 1675 approved the design because “We found it very artificial, proper, and useful.” The tidy three-adjective sentence people quote, and the tour-of-the-cathedral scene around it, cannot be traced to Charles II at all.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Royal warrant approving Wren’s design for the new St Paul’s
Whitehall, 14 May 1675 — “in the 27th Year of Our Reign”
By His Majesty’s command, Henry Coventry (Secretary of State)
Parentalia: or, Memoirs of the Family of the Wrens
1750, London — compiled by the architect’s grandson

source.excerpt: … whereas among divers Designs which have been presented to Us, We have particularly pitched upon one, as well because We found it very artificial, proper, and useful; as because it was so ordered that it might be built and finish’d by Parts: We do therefore by these Presents signify Our Royal Approbation of the said Design … Given at Our Court at Whitehall, the 14th Day of May, 1675, in the 27th Year of Our Reign.
trail: The warrant’s wording was checked directly against the OCR of the 1750 first edition of Parentalia at the Internet Archive ↗, which reads “We found it very artificial, proper, and uſeful” and ends “Given at Our Court at Whitehall, the 14th Day of May, 1675 … By His Majeſty’s Command, Henry Coventry.”

The provenance of the popular version follows Quote Investigator’s survey ↗, which finds the earliest “amusing, awful, and artificial” instance in a 1938 Sunday supplement article, “How Talk Becomes Language”, where the words are credited to King James.

Quote Investigator’s own conclusion is the limit of what can be claimed: there is good evidence Charles II or a representative described the plans as “very artificial, proper, and useful”, while for “awful, amusing and pompous” it has “so far been unable to locate substantive citations in the proper time-period.”
source.excerptNote: Spelling modernised from the 1750 printing, which sets the long ſ (“becauſe”, “uſeful”). The three words that matter — artificial, proper, and useful — are verbatim.

source.rightsNote: The warrant is a 1675 English state document and the text quoted here comes from a book published in London in 1750. Both are far beyond any term of copyright, so the passage is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: King Charles II
author.heading: About King Charles II
author.metaLine: 1630–1685 · King of England, Scotland and Ireland
author.bio: Charles II was restored to the throne in 1660 after the Interregnum, and reigned until his death in 1685. His reign took in the Great Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of London in 1666 — the fire that destroyed old St Paul’s and made Wren’s cathedral necessary. He was a patron of the sciences, chartering the Royal Society, of which Wren was a president.

copyAttribution: King Charles II's royal warrant of 14 May 1675 approved Christopher Wren's design for St Paul's Cathedral because “We found it very artificial, proper, and useful.” The familiar “amusing, awful, and artificial” version is a 20th-century retelling — first printed in 1938, and credited there to King James.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The story is told about four different monarchs, and the adjectives change with the telling. That instability is the clearest sign that the sentence is a retelling rather than a record — and the versions all postdate the reign they describe.

items.tag: Earliest known instance of the famous version
items.why: The first appearance of “amusing, awful, and artificial” located by Quote Investigator ↗ is a 1938 article in the Sunday supplement “This Week Magazine”, which credits King James, not Charles II. Reader’s Digest reprinted it in 1939 and gave it mass circulation.
A 1966 newspaper advertisement in the Times-Picayune of New Orleans gave the three adjectives to Queen Anne, who reigned when the cathedral was completed in 1710.
A 1989 newspaper column on words printed a reader’s note crediting “awful, pompous, and artificial” to William III — a version the science-fiction writer Poul Anderson had used in a 1968 short story.

items.who: the dean and chapter of St Paul’s
items.why: A 1903 history of English churches has the design chosen by the dean because it was “the most awful and artificial” — praise placed in the clergy’s mouths rather than the king’s, and still without a period citation.

misattribution.truthLine: What is documented is narrower and older than the anecdote: a warrant signed at Whitehall on 14 May 1675 approving Wren’s design because “We found it very artificial, proper, and useful” — verifiable in the 1750 Parentalia ↗. Everything else in the story is later.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The anecdote survives because it is a tidy lesson about language drifting under our feet: in the 17th century awful meant awe-inspiring, amusing meant amazing, and artificial meant made with art. All three glosses are sound, which is exactly why the story is so hard to dislodge — the moral is true even though the quotation is not.

The word that genuinely carries the old sense is the one in the warrant. When Charles II’s clerks wrote that the design was “very artificial”, they were calling it skilfully contrived; by 1873 a writer in Fraser’s Magazine had to stop and explain to readers that “the word artificial, we need scarcely explain, then meant artistic.”
detailsBody: St Paul’s was rebuilt between 1675 and 1711 after the old cathedral burned in the Great Fire, a span covering several reigns — which is part of why the tale can be attached to Charles II, James II, William III or Anne without anyone noticing a problem.

The warrant also undercuts the scene the anecdote needs. It approves a design from drawings, before building began, and Wren then altered the scheme heavily as work went on. There was no completed cathedral for a king to tour and pronounce upon in the moment the story describes.
context.pull: The moral of the story is true. The quotation is not.

sourcesVerified.claim: The 1750 Parentalia prints Charles II's warrant of 14 May 1675 approving Wren's design because “We found it very artificial, proper, and useful”, countersigned by Henry Coventry.

Quote Investigator finds the earliest “amusing, awful, and artificial” instance in a 1938 'This Week Magazine' article crediting King James, and says it cannot locate period citations for 'awful, amusing and pompous'.
Charles II lived 29 May 1630 to 6 February 1685 and was King of England, Scotland and Ireland.
Christopher Wren lived 30 October 1632 to 8 March 1723 and designed St Paul’s Cathedral.
St Paul’s Cathedral was rebuilt to Wren’s design after the Great Fire, between 1675 and 1711.
